questions.prompt: What does a qubit's T1 time measure?
options: The characteristic time for a qubit to decay from the excited state back to the ground state (energy relaxation)
The time it takes to perform a single CNOT gate
The total runtime of a quantum algorithm
The number of qubits a quantum computer has
questions.explain: T1 is the energy relaxation time -- how long a qubit prepared in |1> takes to decay back to |0> by losing energy to its environment, as covered in the chapter 1 noise-models lesson.

questions.prompt: Using an illustrative T1 of 100 microseconds and decayProb = 1 - e^(-t/T1), which gate duration from the verified table gives a decoherence probability closest to 0.2% (0.002)?
options: 200 ns
20 ns
50 ns
questions.explain: The verified table gives approximately 1.998 x 10^-3 (about 0.2%) at 200 ns, versus roughly 0.02% at 20 ns, 0.05% at 50 ns, and 1.0% at 1,000 ns.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about the depolarizing noise model are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: Each of the three Pauli errors X, Y, and Z occurs with equal probability p/3
The identity (no error) occurs with probability 1-p
The depolarizing channel treats X errors fundamentally differently from Z errors
At a total error probability of 0.01, each of X, Y, and Z occurs with probability approximately 0.003333
The depolarizing model can only be used to describe two-qubit gate errors, never single-qubit noise
questions.explain: The depolarizing channel splits total error probability p equally among X, Y, Z (each p/3), leaves identity probability at 1-p, and is symmetric across error types -- verified directly: at p=0.01, each Pauli error occurs with probability 0.01/3 = 0.003333.

questions.prompt: What is the standard abbreviation for today's era of noisy, intermediate-scale quantum hardware that is not fault-tolerant?
questions.explain: NISQ (Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum) names the current hardware era, in which decoherence and gate errors (chapter 1) mean devices cannot run long circuits reliably without error correction.

questions.prompt: What does the no-cloning theorem state?
options: No physical process can produce two independent copies of an arbitrary unknown quantum state
Classical bits cannot be duplicated under any circumstances
Qubits can be cloned, but only when they are in a superposition state
Measurement always produces a perfect copy of the measured qubit
questions.explain: No-cloning is the well-established result that no unitary process can copy an arbitrary unknown quantum state, which is exactly why quantum error correction can't use the classical trick of making redundant copies.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are genuine reasons classical error correction (like simple repetition) doesn't port directly to protecting a qubit? (Select all that apply.)
options: Measuring a qubit to check it collapses its superposition, destroying the information being protected
The no-cloning theorem forbids copying an arbitrary unknown quantum state
Quantum computers are physically incapable of running any error-correcting code
Qubits can only ever be in the state |0> or |1>, never a superposition
Quantum errors include continuous small rotations, not just discrete flips
questions.explain: The real obstacles are measurement collapse, no-cloning, and the continuous nature of quantum errors -- not that quantum computers can't run error correction at all (they can, as chapter 3 shows) or that qubits can't hold superpositions (they can, by definition).

questions.prompt: A classical code has minimum distance 5. Using the rule t = floor((d-1)/2), how many errors can it correct?
questions.explain: floor((5-1)/2) = floor(4/2) = 2, matching the 5-bit repetition code's verified behavior of tolerating up to 2 simultaneous bit flips.

questions.prompt: Using the verified majority-vote success formula, what is the success probability (to 3 decimal places) of the 3-bit classical repetition code at a channel bit-flip rate of p=0.10?
questions.explain: The verified computation gives P(success) = 0.972000 at p=0.10 for the 3-bit repetition code, versus 0.900000 with no code at all.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about the 3-qubit bit-flip code are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: It encodes logical |0> as |000> and logical |1> as |111>
Its stabilizer generators are Z1Z2 and Z2Z3
It can correct any single Z (phase-flip) error
It can correct any single X (bit-flip) error on exactly one of its 3 qubits
It requires 5 physical qubits per logical qubit
questions.explain: The bit-flip code uses 3 (not 5) physical qubits, encodes via |000>/|111>, uses stabilizers Z1Z2 and Z2Z3, and corrects any single X error -- but it is blind to Z errors, as the verified syndrome table shows.

questions.prompt: Starting from logical |1>_L = |111> in the 3-qubit bit-flip code, an X error strikes qubit 2, producing the verified syndrome (Z1Z2, Z2Z3) = (1,1). What correction should be applied?
options: Flip qubit 2
Flip qubit 1
Flip qubit 3
No correction needed
questions.explain: The verified syndrome table maps (1,1) uniquely to an error on qubit 2 -- flipping it back restores the state to |111>.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about the Shor 9-qubit code are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: It uses the phase-flip code as the outer code and the bit-flip code as the inner code
It requires 3x3=9 physical qubits to protect 1 logical qubit
It was the first code proven to correct an arbitrary single-qubit Pauli error
It is the code used by essentially all real fault-tolerant hardware roadmaps today
It can correct X, Y, and Z errors, but only if they occur on multiple qubits simultaneously
questions.explain: The Shor code concatenates an outer phase-flip code with an inner bit-flip code (3x3=9 qubits) and was the historic first proof of general single-qubit QEC -- but real hardware roadmaps favor the surface code (chapter 5), and the Shor code corrects a single arbitrary error on one qubit, not simultaneous multi-qubit errors.

questions.prompt: How many total physical qubits does the Shor code use to protect exactly 1 logical qubit against an arbitrary single-qubit error?
questions.explain: 3 outer phase-flip blocks x 3 inner bit-flip qubits per block = 9 total physical qubits, verified directly from the concatenated construction.

questions.prompt: In the ancilla-based circuit measuring the Z1Z2 stabilizer, what does measuring the ancilla in the Z basis actually reveal?
options: Whether qubits 1 and 2 agree or disagree, without revealing the encoded logical amplitudes alpha and beta
The exact values of alpha and beta encoded in the logical qubit
Nothing at all; the ancilla measurement has no relationship to the data qubits
Whether qubit 3 has experienced any error
questions.explain: Because Z1Z2 has the same +1 eigenvalue on both logical basis states, the ancilla measurement can only reveal an error-induced disagreement between qubits 1 and 2, never the encoded amplitudes -- this is exactly why syndrome measurement respects no-cloning.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are true about the Steane [[7,1,3]] code? (Select all that apply.)
options: It has 6 stabilizer generators: 3 X-type and 3 Z-type
It is built from the classical Hamming(7,4) code's parity-check matrix
It requires more physical qubits than the Shor code for the same single-error protection
Its logical Hadamard, X, Z, and CNOT gates can be applied transversally
Its minimum distance is 7, matching its total qubit count
questions.explain: The Steane code uses 7 qubits (fewer than the Shor code's 9) with 6 stabilizers built from Hamming(7,4), supports transversal Clifford gates, and has minimum distance 3 (not 7) -- it is [[7,1,3]] notation, not a code with distance equal to its qubit count.

questions.prompt: An X error strikes qubit 3 of the Steane code. Using column 3 of the parity-check matrix H, which is [0,1,1], what is the resulting Z-type syndrome (rows 1, 2, 3)?
questions.explain: Reading column 3 of H directly gives the Z-type syndrome (0,1,1) -- rows 2 and 3 flip because qubit 3 participates in those stabilizers, row 1 doesn't, verified directly via the column-lookup method.

questions.prompt: The Steane code has n=7 physical qubits and k=1 logical qubit. Using the n-k rule for stabilizer generator count, how many independent stabilizer generators does it have?
questions.explain: n - k = 7 - 1 = 6, matching the Steane code's verified 3 X-type plus 3 Z-type stabilizer generators.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are true about the general CSS code construction? (Select all that apply.)
options: It is built from a pair of classical codes C1 and C2
The nesting condition (C2's dual is a subset of C1) must hold for the resulting stabilizers to commute
X-type stabilizers come from C1's structure, Z-type stabilizers from C2's structure
C1 and C2 must always be two completely different classical codes
The surface code is not built using the CSS construction
questions.explain: CSS codes use a pair of nested classical codes to build commuting X-type and Z-type stabilizers; C1 and C2 can be the same code (as in the self-dual Steane code) or different; and the surface code is itself also a CSS code, built on a 2D lattice.

questions.prompt: Why does it matter for real hardware that every surface-code stabilizer touches only 4 physically neighboring qubits, rather than arbitrary non-adjacent qubits?
options: It matches how real qubit platforms are wired, where each qubit only interacts with its nearest neighbors, avoiding a need for long-range connectivity
It has no practical significance and is purely a mathematical convenience
It means the surface code requires fewer total physical qubits than every other known code
It eliminates the need for any ancilla qubits during syndrome extraction
questions.explain: Nearest-neighbor-only stabilizers are one of the three concrete properties (chapter 5) that make the surface code practical on real hardware, which typically only wires each qubit to its immediate physical neighbors.

questions.prompt: Using the verified formula total = 2d^2 - 1, how many total physical qubits does a distance-9 rotated surface code require to encode 1 logical qubit?
questions.explain: 2(9^2) - 1 = 2(81) - 1 = 161, matching the verified surface-code qubit-count table.

questions.prompt: Which properties make the surface code favorable for real hardware? (Select all that apply.)
options: Its stabilizers only require nearest-neighbor connectivity on a 2D grid
It has a comparatively favorable error threshold among practical code families
Its stabilizers are low-weight, touching only 4 qubits in the bulk
It requires fewer physical qubits per logical qubit than every other known code at every distance
It has already been run at the scale needed for useful fault-tolerant algorithms
questions.explain: The three real advantages are connectivity, threshold, and low-weight local stabilizers -- the surface code actually needs more qubits than the Steane code at small distances, and useful-scale fault tolerance has not yet been achieved.

questions.prompt: A particular stabilizer's measured outcome flips in round 7, then reverts to normal in round 8, with no correction applied in between. Based on the distinction between real data errors and faulty measurement rounds, what is the most likely explanation?
options: A faulty ancilla measurement in round 7, since real data errors persist across rounds until corrected
A real data error that happened to spontaneously self-correct without any intervention
Evidence that the surface code's threshold theorem is false
Proof that the decoder has made zero computational errors
questions.explain: Real data errors cause a stabilizer outcome to flip and stay flipped until corrected; an isolated single-round flip that reverts on its own is the signature of a faulty ancilla measurement, not a genuine data error.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are true about minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) decoding of the surface code? (Select all that apply.)
options: It treats persistent syndrome defects as nodes in a graph to be paired up
It pairs defects (or a defect with the lattice boundary) to minimize total pairing cost
It requires no knowledge of which stabilizers flipped across multiple rounds, only the final round
Decoding speed, not just accuracy, is an important and still-active engineering challenge
MWPM was invented specifically and exclusively for the surface code, with no prior classical use
questions.explain: MWPM pairs defects using multi-round spacetime syndrome data (not just the final round), reuses a pre-existing classical graph algorithm, and decoding latency at scale remains an open, active engineering challenge.

questions.prompt: Using total = 2d^2 - 1, how many physical qubits per logical qubit does a distance-15 surface code require?
questions.explain: 2(15^2) - 1 = 2(225) - 1 = 449, matching the verified surface-code cost table used throughout chapter 6.

questions.prompt: An algorithm needs 50 logical qubits, each protected at code distance 11 (241 physical qubits per logical qubit). What is the total physical-qubit cost for the base error-correcting code?
questions.explain: 50 x 241 = 12,050, computed directly using the two-step resource-estimation method from chapter 6's lab.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are true statements about the error threshold theorem? (Select all that apply.)
options: Below the threshold p_th, increasing code distance exponentially suppresses the logical error rate
At or above p_th, increasing code distance does not help, and can make the logical error rate worse
The existence of a threshold for code families like the surface code is a proven theoretical result
This course states a specific, settled numerical threshold value achieved by current real hardware
The threshold theorem guarantees fault tolerance regardless of a device's actual physical error rate
questions.explain: The theorem's existence and its below/above-threshold asymmetry are proven and well-established; this course deliberately avoids asserting a specific settled numerical threshold for real hardware, and the theorem's benefit is conditional on actually operating below threshold, not automatic.

questions.prompt: Chapter 6 presents two numbers: a cited estimate of roughly 20 million physical qubits to break RSA-2048 with Shor's algorithm, and an illustrative example of 44,900 physical qubits for a hypothetical 100-logical-qubit scenario at distance 15. How should these two numbers be understood?
options: As two distinct things -- a literature citation reflecting a detailed real-algorithm analysis, versus a simplified worked arithmetic example meant to show the estimation method
As the same number, just rounded differently for presentation
As proof that the illustrative example is more accurate than the published literature estimate
As evidence that resource estimation is purely guesswork with no real method behind it
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly separates a cited literature estimate (Gidney & Ekera, accounting for real algorithm structure and distillation overhead) from its own simplified illustrative multiplication, to avoid conflating the two.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are true about fault-tolerant gate sets? (Select all that apply.)
options: Clifford gates (X, Z, H, CNOT) can be applied transversally on codes like the Steane code and surface code
The Gottesman-Knill theorem shows Clifford-only circuits can be efficiently simulated classically
The T gate can generally be applied transversally on these codes at the fidelity needed for fault tolerance
Magic-state distillation is used to supply high-fidelity T gates despite the transversality limitation
Universal quantum computation can be achieved using only Clifford gates
questions.explain: Clifford gates are transversal and classically simulable in combination (Gottesman-Knill), which is exactly why a non-Clifford gate like T is needed for universality -- but T resists transversal implementation, so magic-state distillation supplies it instead.

questions.prompt: The well-known magic-state distillation protocol referenced in this course consumes how many noisy input magic states to produce 1 higher-fidelity output state?
questions.explain: The 15-to-1 protocol consumes 15 noisy magic states to output 1 state of substantially higher fidelity, usable via gate teleportation to apply a high-fidelity logical T gate.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical algorithm needs 20 logical qubits, each protected at code distance 27 (1,457 physical qubits per logical qubit). What is the total physical-qubit cost for the base error-correcting code?
questions.explain: 20 x 1,457 = 29,140, computed directly using the same two-step resource-estimation method applied throughout chapters 6 and 7.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are part of this course's honest framing of the NISQ era versus the fault-tolerant era? (Select all that apply.)
options: No quantum computer has yet run a classically-infeasible, practically useful algorithm end-to-end in the fault-tolerant regime
NISQ-era hardware runs without full error correction, limiting it to noise-tolerant algorithm classes
The surface code is the leading practical candidate, but running it at useful scale remains a forward-looking goal
Fault-tolerant quantum computing at useful scale has already been achieved as of this course
The transition from NISQ to fault tolerance is considered a nearly solved, minor remaining engineering step
questions.explain: The course's explicit honesty checkpoint (chapter 7) states that no useful algorithm has run fault-tolerantly yet, NISQ hardware lacks full error correction, and the surface code remains a leading but unproven-at-scale candidate -- it explicitly rejects framing fault tolerance as already achieved or nearly solved.
